## Why this is in my notes at all

I got roped into the school's working group on generative AI. Draft policy AIP-2025-03, first meeting 12 March 2025, chaired by the deputy principal, Gráinne Kehoe. Five of us: me, two from English, one from Computer Science, and Paul from the parents' association. These notes are my thinking, not the policy.

## The essay problem

A second-year essay on the Somme came in last November with a quotation from "Captain Edward Thornbury, 1st Dublin Fusiliers". No such person. The student had asked a chatbot for "a primary source quote" and got a fluent fabrication. He wasn't trying to cheat; he didn't know it could make things up. That is the real lesson, and it's a history lesson: provenance.

We tried two AI detectors on 30 essays I knew were written by hand in class. One flagged 4 of them as "likely AI". All four were by students with English as a second language. We dropped the detectors that week.

## Leaving Cert reform

The redeveloped senior cycle subjects bring in Additional Assessment Components, worth 40% in the new specifications, done over months outside the exam hall. History is in a later tranche, but the worry is the same: if a big share of the grade is coursework, how do we know whose work it is? My view: more in-class drafting, oral defence of the project (ten minutes, "talk me through your sources"), and keep the research log.

## Bias and fairness

- ProPublica, "Machine Bias", May 2016, on the COMPAS risk scores in Broward County: black defendants who did not reoffend were almost twice as likely to be flagged high risk as white ones.
- The Amazon recruiting tool scrapped in 2018 after it learnt to downgrade CVs mentioning "women's". Relevant to anyone writing a [[Hiring loop rubric]].
- The counter-argument (Kleinberg et al., 2016): several fairness measures can't all be satisfied at once unless base rates are equal. So "unbiased" has to be defined before it can be demanded.

## Alignment

Stuart Russell, *Human Compatible* (2019), p. 172: a system given a fixed objective has a reason to stop you switching it off, because it can't achieve the objective if it's off. His fix is to make the machine uncertain about what we want. The King Midas problem, as he calls it. I'd add that a teacher knows this already: set a fixed target and students hit the target, not the learning.

## Consequences versus rights

The utilitarian framing ("maximise expected benefit") dominates the industry. See [[Utilitarianism]] for why I'm wary. The [[Trolley problem]] gets dragged in for self-driving cars, mostly unhelpfully: the real ethical questions are about who carries the risk and who decides, not about split-second swerves.

## The EU AI Act

- Entered into force 1 August 2024.
- Prohibited practices apply from 2 February 2025. Emotion recognition in workplaces and schools is on the banned list, which matters for those "engagement monitoring" products being sold to schools.
- Education is a high-risk area under Annex III, point 3: systems that decide admission or grade students.
- Obligations for general-purpose models from 2 August 2025.

## What I tell students

1. It is a very confident guesser. Check every name, date and quote against a real source.
2. Say when you used it and for what. Hiding it is the offence, not using it.
3. Your own bad first draft is worth more to you than its good one.

Next working-group meeting: 23 April 2025. My action: draft the student-facing one-pager, max 300 words.
